title: My family — and an upside-down "have"
goal: Introduce your family, say what and whom you have, and get your head around two confusing things at once: possessives that follow the gender of the thing owned, and a "have" sentence that is built the other way around from English.
bekal: name the members of your immediate family
use мой / моя / моё / мои correctly
say "I have …" with У меня есть …
say you don't have something with У меня нет …

dialogs.title: Диалог — A photo in the wallet
dialogs.intro: Ani and Марко are sitting in the campus canteen. Марко takes out his phone and shows a family photo. Notice that the word "have" never appears in the Russian — what appears instead is the word "at".

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: What a big family! Who's this?

lines.speaker: Марко:
lines.id: This is my dad and my mom. And these are my sisters.
lines.literal: this — my (masc) — dad — and — my (fem) — mom. and — this — my (pl) — sisters.

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: How many sisters do you have?

lines.speaker: Марко:
lines.id: I have three sisters and one brother. And you?
lines.literal: at — me — three — sister — and — one — brother. and — at — you?

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: I have an older brother. No sisters.
lines.literal: at — me — is — older — brother. sister — there-is-none.

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: No, he's an engineer. He works in Jakarta.
lines.literal: no, he — engineer. he — works — in — Jakarta.

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: My dad is a teacher, and my mom stays at home.
lines.literal: my — dad — teacher, whereas — mom — at-home.

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: No, but we have a cat. Her name is Luna.
lines.literal: no, but — at — us — is — cat. her (object) — they-call — Luna.

notes: **"I have" in Russian is "at me there is".** ⚠️ This is one of the strangest constructions for English speakers. *У меня есть брат* is literally "at me is brother". **The subject of the sentence is not me but the brother** — which is why the noun stays in its dictionary form, while "I" turns into меня.

**Есть can be dropped when existence isn't the point.** *У меня есть брат* stresses that the brother **exists**. But once we know he exists and we're describing him, есть disappears: *У меня **старший** брат* — my brother is older. A rule of thumb for A1: use есть when answering "do you have one or not", drop it when explaining "what kind you have".

**To say you don't have something, use нет — and the noun changes too.** *У меня **нет** сестр**ы*** — I don't have a sister. Literally "at me there-is-none of-sister". ⚠️ After нет the noun **must** go into the genitive: сестра → сестры, брат → брата, время → времени. This is the second use of the genitive you've met, after из in Unit 3.

**Possessives follow the gender of the THING owned, not the owner.** ⚠️ This is the second big trap in this unit. In English "my" never changes: my book, my sister, my house. In Russian: *мой брат* (masc), *моя сестра* (fem), *моё окно* (neuter), *мои сёстры* (plural). What decides is the word after it, not who is speaking.

**Его, её, их never change.** A little gift: the third-person possessives are fixed. *его брат*, *его сестра*, *его окно* — all его. Same for её (her) and их (their). So of the six owners, three need no forms memorized at all.

**Отец/мать are formal, папа/мама everyday.** Adults use both. Отец and мать sound a bit more distant and often appear in documents; папа and мама are what people of any age use in normal conversation. ⚠️ Remember: **папа** ends in -а but is still masculine — *мой папа*, not *моя папа*.
**Какая большая семья! is an exclamation pattern.** Какой / какая / какое / какие + adjective = "what a …!". *Какой красивый город!* — what a beautiful city!

grammars.title: Possessives — the table you need to master
body: The rows are the owners, the columns are the gender of the thing owned. Only the first three rows change.
after: Look at the pattern, not each cell: the masculine form ends in a consonant or **-й**, the feminine in **-а/-я**, the neuter in **-ё/-е**, the plural in **-и**. The same pattern comes back with adjectives (Unit 16).
⚠️ **его** is pronounced *ye-VO*, not *ye-GO*. The г in the endings -его/-ого always sounds like *v*.

grammars.title: У меня есть — the "have" sentence
body: The order is fixed: **У + person (object form) + есть + thing (dictionary form)**.

head: Who
Form after У
Example
rows: У меня есть брат. — I have a brother.
У тебя есть время? — Do you have time?
У него есть машина. — He has a car.
У неё есть собака. — She has a dog.
У нас есть кошка. — We have a cat.
У вас есть вопрос? — Do you have a question?
У них есть дом. — They have a house.

after: ⚠️ After a preposition, его/её/их add an **н**: его → у **н**его, её → у **н**её, их → у **н**их. This applies after every preposition, not just у.
To negate: replace **есть** with **нет** and put the thing in the genitive. *У меня есть брат* → *У меня **нет брата***. *У неё есть собака* → *У неё **нет собаки***.

blocks.title: What has no exact match
items: Like English, Russian has **no separate words for older and younger siblings**. Брат means brother, full stop. If age matters, add **старший** (older) or **младший** (younger): *старший брат* = older brother.

On the other hand, Russian has something English lacks: the **отчество**, a middle name made from the father's name. Иван Петрович means "Ivan, son of Pyotr". Addressing someone by first name + отчество (*Ольга Петровна*) is the everyday respectful form — roughly like "Mrs. …", but warmer and used far more widely.
Children also use **дядя** and **тётя** for adults they don't know — much like kids in many English-speaking families call family friends "uncle" and "auntie".

exercises.prompt: Fill in мой, моя, моё or мои.
Make the sentences negative. Remember the genitive ending.
items: У меня есть брат. → У меня ____
У неё есть собака. → У неё ____
У нас есть машина. → У нас ____
У него есть сестра. → У него ____
У вас есть время. → У вас ____

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.

answers: мой — моя — моё — мои — мой — моя
нет брата — нет собаки — нет машины — нет сестры — нет времени
У меня есть брат. — Это моя семья. — Сколько у вас сестёр? — Он инженер. — У нас есть кошка.
Это моя семья. — У меня есть старший брат. — У меня нет сестры. — Мой папа учитель. — У вас есть собака? — У нас есть кошка.
